newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-French industry output rise gives boost.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-French industry output rise gives boost.

text.p: A far stronger than expected rebound in April manufacturing output revived hopes the French economy is gathering steam, giving a boost to the new Socialist government, economists said.

The economy grew by a lacklustre 0.2 percent in the first three months of the year but economists said a third straight monthly increase in manufacturing output, giving a rise of 3.7 percent from 1996, suggested the worst was over.

French statistics institute INSEE said manufacturing output climbed 1.1 percent in April while the broad measure of industrial production, which accounts for about 40 percent of gross domestic product, jumped three percent.
While the rise in the broad measure was far higher than a 0.4 percent increase forecast by economists, a 14.8 percent surge in energy output inflated the headline figure by 1.8 percentage points.

"It's a good report because an increase in 1.1 percent is the sort of increase you just don't get very often and because it comes as the third consecutive monthly rise," said Nomura International bond analyst Sonja Gibbs. "Ultimately you cannot have such strength in exports without it working through to the domestic economy in some way."

Exports were the driving force of French growth in the first quarter of 1997 and the last three months of 1996, up 1.1 percent and 1.5 percent respectively, and economists said the 12 percent decline in the franc against the dollar so far this year would continue to help exporters.

Solid growth in 1997 is a key factor for France to bring down its public deficit to near three percent of gross domestic product, the strict target for joining monetary union, especially given a series of new spending measures unveiled by Prime Minister Lionel Jospin on Thursday.

However, some economists cautioned that although the rebound in manufacturing activity was positive it really only made official growth forecasts look a little more realistic after the weak start to the year.

"It's good news but it was needed. I seen no reason to upgrade forecasts, it's a first step in justifying (growth) forecasts above two percent this year," Joanne Perez, strategist at Merrill Lynch said. "We still need momentum from investment in the second half."

The previous centre-right coalition forecast growth of 2.3 percent this year but many private economists expect growth to reach barely 2.0 percent unless French companies, wary of the weakness of domestic demand, take the plunge and start investing and restocking inventories.

Economists said France's dependence on exports was highlighted in Friday's industrial production report by the fact sectors depending largely on domestic demand had not seen such large increases in output.

"This number gives a deformed view of the economy," said Herve Goulletquer, economist at Credit Lyonnais. "Without exports, economic growth would not be what it is today...The question is whether the manufacturing strength can be spread to other sectors."
